Non-targeted facilitation of primary sludge anaerobic fermentation by 
micro-aeration and the simultaneous nutrients transformations 
Caihong Liu a, Tanglong Zhang a, Lin Li a,*, Shaowu Liu b, Jingjun Bo a, Mohammed Mouhib c, 
Qiang He a,* 
a Key Laboratory of the Three Gorges Reservoir Region’s Eco-environment, Ministry of Education, College of Environment and Ecology, Chongqing University, Chongqing 
400045, China 
b Chongqing Water Group Co., Ltd., Chongqing 400000, China 
c Institute of Chemical Sciences and Engineering (ISIC), Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne (EPFL), 1015 Lausanne, Switzerland   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Volatile fatty acid 
P and N transformation 
Sludge 
Microbial functions 
Resource recovery 
A B S T R A C T   
Anaerobic fermentation is a widely used technology for resource recovery from municipal sludge (e.g., primary 
sludge). Micro-aeration is an emerging strategy which can be incorporated into this technology. However, the 
effect of micro-aeration on the anaerobic fermentation performance and the nutrients transformations are not 
well known. This study investigated the impact of micro-aeration on the production of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) 
from primary sludge as well as the simultaneous nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) transformations in the system. 
The obtained results indicated that application of micro-aeration improved the microbial activities and facili­
tated all the hydrolysis, acetogenesis and methanogenesis processes. Hydrogenotrophic methanogen was 
enriched by micro-aeration while the acetoclastic methanogenesis was still the dominant CH4 production 
pathway at gene level. The concentration of VFAs was lower with micro-aeration than in the control system, 
which could be attributed to the enhanced consumption of VFAs. The simultaneous transformations of N and P 
were observed with different patterns. Micro-aeration led to removal of up to 131.6 mg/L of N, with occurrence 
of nitrification and denitrification found to be responsible for the N removal. In contrast, the total P content 
remained unchanged in the reactor. However, micro-aeration was found to inhibit both extracellular organic-P 
mineralization and intracellular poly-P degradation, resulting in lower soluble PO4
3−-P and more P distributed in 
the organic-P fraction in solid phase. This study provides novel insights into the microscopic mechanisms of the 
micro-aeration on anaerobic fermentation and the simultaneous regulation of N and P release.   
1. Introduction 
Resource recovery from municipal sludge is of great importance 
considering that treatment and disposal of sludge account for approxi­
mately 20–60 % of the operating costs of wastewater treatment plants 
(WWTPs) [63]. Anaerobic fermentation is widely used in sludge stabi­
lization and resource recovery (e.g., in the form of volatile fatty acid 
(VFA)). As an important component of WWTP sludge, primary sludge 
contains a large fraction of readily bioavailable organic matters, which 
result in efficient VFA production compared to waste activated sludge 
[30]. The obtained fermentation broth rich in VFA can be used as the 
carbon source for wastewater treatment or biosynthesis of other value- 
added commodities [49,52]. 
In order to facilitate the hydrolysis step and enhance the VFA 
production during anaerobic fermentation, various research have been 
carried out on operational parameters optimization (e.g., temperature, 
sludge retention time (SRT)) as well as application of pretreatment 
methods (e.g., ultrasound, thermal hydrolysis) [9,37]. For example, 
Wang et al. found that lower temperatures (20–35 ◦C) were not 
conducive to VFA production in two-phase reactors, mainly due to 
resulting lower microbial and enzyme activities [47]. Miron et al. found 
that a shorter SRT (<8d) was more favorable for VFA production from 
primary sludge [33], which was also supported by Yuan et al. [59]. 
Beside operating parameters optimization, VFA production could also be 
enhanced by applying physical pretreatment such as ultrasound [19] 
and thermal hydrolysis [34]. Chemical methods such as acid [6] and 
alkali pretreatment [38,39] have also been explored to improve VFA 
production. However, these pretreatment methods often require

intensive energy input or the addition of extra chemicals, thus leading to 
increased operating costs and production of chemical wastes [52]. 
Alternatively, apart from the above-mentioned methods, micro- 
aeration is an emerging strategy used in anaerobic fermentation, due 
to its environmental friendliness and economic efficiency [10]. The 
presence of oxygen has been shown to enhance the activity and diversity 
of facultative microorganisms which utilizing O2 as the electron 
acceptor [24]. Lim et al. found that micro-aeration increased the 
abundances of phyla Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes to 72 % and 24 % 
respectively, leading to enhanced hydrolysis efficiency due to extracel­
lular hydrolase secreted by Firmicutes [24]. In addition, reactive oxygen 
species induced by micro-aeration can also promote the intracellular 
enzyme activity of microorganisms [60]. An et al. studied the hydrolysis 
kinetics of industrial park wastewater with limited aeration, and found 
that the introduction of oxygen increased the reaction rate (k parameter) 
by 80.8 % compared to the control group [2]. It has been reported in 
most studies to reduce the accumulation of VFA and increase CH4 pro­
duction [35]. In contrast, some other studies also reported that intro­
duction of oxygen can inhibit the growth of methanogens, avoiding VFA 
being consumed by methanogens [52,58]. The primary sludge contains 
a high portion of organic matter and was reported to be more biode­
gradable than waste activated sludge [53], but the effects of micro- 
aeration on its VFA production performance remains unclear. In addi­
tion, a large amount of nitrogen and phosphorus would be released 
during anaerobic fermentation, which can increase the N and P load 
during its subsequent utilization (e.g., as carbon source for wastewater 
treatment) [29]. Biological N and P removal during wastewater treat­
ment depend on alternating anaerobic and aerobic conditions, which is 
commonly realized in separate bioreactors [4,17]. Hence, nitrification 
and P uptake are not expected to happen during anaerobic fermentation, 
resulting in high NH4
+-N and PO4
3−-P accumulation. But micro-aeration 
could introduce aerobic micro-regions under the anaerobic environ­
ment, in which nitrification and P release might happen [21]. Never­
theless, the existing researches primarily focused on the anaerobic 
fermentation performance while overlooked the simultaneous trans­
formations of soluble N and P [23,58]. Therefore, the impact of micro- 
aeration on primary sludge fermentation as well as the accompanying 
N and P transformations needs to be comprehensively investigated to 
advance this strategy towards better application. 
Based on the above information, this study aims to explore the effects 
of micro-aeration on anaerobic fermentation of primary sludge and the 
mechanism of N and P transformations. The effects of micro-aeration on 
organic matters solubilization, N and P transformation and VFA pro­
duction performance during primary sludge fermentation were charac­
terized using batch and semi-continuous experiment. To this end, the 
activity variations of key enzymes involved in hydrolysis, acetogenesis 
and methanogenesis steps were investigated with and without micro- 
aeration. Finally, metagenomic analysis was used to reveal the mecha­
nism of observed changes at a gene level. Altogether, these findings 
provide an in-depth understanding of the effect of micro-aeration on 
anaerobic fermentation systems and the underlying mechanism. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Source of primary sludge and inoculum 
The primary sludge was obtained from the primary sedimentation 
tank of a full-scale WWTP in Chongqing, China. The obtained primary 
sludge was screened through an 8-mesh sieve to remove large inorganic 
substances, and stored at 4 ◦C before use. The inoculum sludge was 
obtained from a semi-continuous anaerobic fermentation reactor for 
VFAs production, which was operated steadily at 37 ◦C with an SRT of 6 
days, and mechanical stirring of 100 rpm. The main characteristics of 
primary sludge and inoculum are reported in Table S1 (Supporting In­
formation, SI). 
2.2. Batch experimental setup 
The batch experiments were conducted in 2 sets of serum bottles, 
which compromised a control, and a micro-aeration group. Each serum 
bottle (500 mL working volume) was connected to a gas bag and fed 
with 400 mL of primary sludge. Bottles without aeration were prepared 
as control group. Micro-aeration was realized using a peristaltic pump 
connected to the bottle, and operated to supply 0.001 vvm (i.e., 4 mL/ 
min) of air based on previous study [52]. After flushing with N2 for 5 
min, all the bottles were sealed and placed in a water bath shaker at 
37 ◦C and 100 rpm for 9 days. Gas and liquid samples were collected by a 
syringe every day for gas components and other determinations. 
2.3. Operation of semi-continuous reactors 
The semi-continuous experiment was conducted in 2 continuous 
stirred tank reactors (CSTR) (working volume of 4 L) made of plexiglass 
to study the long-term influence of micro-aeration. Water bath was 
designed to maintain the temperature around 37 ◦C during the 
fermentation. The aeration diffuser was placed at the bottom of the 
reactor, and micro-aeration was achieved same to the bath experiment. 
The reactor with micro-aeration was the experimental reactor (micro- 
aeration), and the reactor without micro-aeration was set as the control. 
During the operation, mechanical stirring was applied at 100 rpm with 
an agitator. The ORP (oxidation–reduction potential) probe was used to 
monitor the variations of oxidation reduction potential in the reactor. 
Initially, 3 L of primary sludge was fed into the reactor, and then 1 L of 
primary sludge was discharged and fed daily. The liquid and gas samples 
were collected regularly for further analysis. The sludge samples on day 
30 were collected for metagenomic and real-time quantitative PCR (RT- 
qPCR) analysis. 
2.4. Analytical methods 
Total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), chemical oxygen demand 
(COD), NH4
+-N, NO3
−-N, NO2
−-N, and PO4
3−-P were measured according to 
standard methods [3]. The total organic carbon (TOC) was analyzed 
using a TOC analyzer (Shimadzu TOC-L CPH, Japan). Soluble poly­
saccharide content was determined by the anthrone-sulfuric acid 
method with glucose as the standard. Soluble protein concentration was 
determined using a BCA protein determination kit (Beijing Suolaibao 
Technology Co., Ltd). CH4, NO2, and NO contents in the gas phase were 
determined using a gas chromatography (GC1690, Hangzhou Jiedao, 
China) with a capillary column and a flame ionization detector (FID). 
VFAs were determined by a gas chromatography (GC7900, Tianmei, 
China) with a TM-FFAP column (30 m × 0.32 mm (ID) × 0.5 μm) column 
and a FID detector. The determination of enzyme activities and excita­
tion emission matrix (EEM) fluorescence spectra was detailed in Text S1 
(SI). Detailed extraction protocol of P was provided in Text S2 (SI). 
2.5. Metagenomic sequencing, RT-qPCR and 16S rRNA gene sequencing 
The metagenomic sequencing were conducted by Majorbio Bio- 
pharm Technology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Samples were stored at 
−80 ◦C before test. The genomic DNA was extracted using an E.Z.N.A 
®soil kit (Omega Bio tek, USA). The concentration and purity of ob­
tained DNA samples was assessed using an ultra-micro spectrophotom­
eter (NanoDrop2000, USA), and 1 % agarose gel electrophoresis. 
Extracted DNA was broken into fragments of around 400 bp, and 
sequencing library was constructed using the NEXTFLEX™ Rapid DNA- 
Seq Kit. Samples were sequenced on an Illumina platform with Illumina 
NovaSeq Reagent Kits. The obtained data was analyzed in the online 
Majorbio Cloud Platform (https://www.majorbio.com). RT-qPCR and 
16S rRNA gene sequencing are detailed in Text S3 and Text S4 (SI).

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. VFAs production and organics dissolution of the batch experiment 
3.1.1. VFAs production from primary sludge 
Variations of VFAs concentration and distribution during the 
anaerobic fermentation are shown in Fig. 1. In the control group 
(Fig. 1a), the VFAs concentrations increased initially and reached a peak 
of 2094.7 mg COD/L on day 6, and then gradually decreased to 1534.4 
mg COD/L on day 9 possibly owing to the activities of methanogens 
[33]. In contrast, in the micro-aeration group, the VFA production 
reached the maximal value of 1662.5 mg COD/L on the first day, fol­
lowed by a slow decrease (437.3 mg COD/L on day 9). This trend 
indicated that the micro-aeration posed adverse effects on VFAs accu­
mulation during the anaerobic fermentation process. The consumption 
of VFAs further resulted in rising pH values, creating a suitable envi­
ronment for methanogens to grow [23]. Therefore, VFAs would be 
further consumed over time to form CH4 as time extended. 
To further explore the fermentation performance, VFAs distribution 
and SCOD composition were explored. It was found that VFAs were the 
main organic component accounting for more than 57 % of the SCOD in 
the batch experiments (Fig. 1d), which was also observed in a previous 
study [25]. Variations of VFA distributions in the control and micro- 
aeration groups are illustrated in Fig. 1b, c. Acetate and propionate 
were the dominant VFAs produced during the fermentation in both 
groups, in agreement with previous literature [45]. In the control group, 
the acetate abundance increased to 53 % on day 4 and subsequently 
exhibited a gradual decline to 42 %, while propionate abundance fluc­
tuated around 20 % during the whole reaction. In contrast, the acetate 
abundance decreased significantly from 48 % to around 27 % in the 
micro-aeration group. It might be attributed to that acetate was more 
easily utilized by bacteria [50]. As acetate decreased, the propionate 
abundance in this group gradually increased from 19 % to 32 % on day 
4, and then began to decline to 15 % over time. The abundances of iso- 
valerate, butyrate, and iso-butyrate all showed an increase over time, 
which was possibly owing to the rapid consumption of acetate and 
propionate with micro-aeration. 
3.1.2. Characteristics of the dissolved organic matters 
Generally, the anaerobic fermentation includes hydrolysis, acido­
genesis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis, and hydrolysis is widely 
accepted as the rate-limiting step [12,56]. To understand how micro- 
aeration affects the dissolution of organics from sludge solids, the con­
centrations of carbohydrates and proteins in the soluble fraction were 
determined under different operation conditions (micro-aeration and 
control) (Fig. 2). The soluble carbohydrates accumulated during the first 
several days in both groups. In the control group (Fig. 2a), it increased 
from an initial 15.2 mg COD/L to 36.1 mg COD/L, followed by a rapid 
decrease from day 8. The introduction of micro-aeration significantly 
increased carbohydrate release, which achieved the maximal value 
(76.3 mg COD/L) on day 5 (Fig. 2b). Conversely, a different variation 
pattern was observed for protein concentrations over time. While the 
protein concentration reached its maximum of 1152.5 mg COD/L on day 
6 in the control group, protein concentrations in the micro-aeration 
group peaked sooner (day 2) at lower values (692.0 mg COD/L). This 
might be attributed to released proteins being rapidly consumed by 
microorganisms. It can be concluded that the micro-aeration facilitated 
the release and conversion of the organic matters especially proteins.

SCOD compositions.

To explore the spectral difference of solubilized organics between 
these two groups, EEM spectra of the supernatant on day 3 were ob­
tained (Fig. 2c, d). The EEM spectrum was divided into five regions 
based on excitation wavelength (EX) and emission wavelength (EM) 
[5,13,44]. It was found that the main soluble organics with and without 
micro-aeration were mainly simple aromatic proteins (region I and II) 
and soluble microbial products (SMP, region IV). SMP are mainly 
composed of microbial metabolites such as carbohydrate and proteins, 
which were widely observed in anaerobic fermentation systems [52,55].

While region I and II accounted for most of the fluorescence signal in 
both control and the micro-aeration groups, the fluorescent abundance 
of region II was much higher in the micro-aeration group (48 %) than the 
control group (35 %). The fluorescence of region IV (SMP) also increased 
from 6 % (control) to 13 % (micro-aeration). These observations indi­
cated that the micro-aeration induced enhanced solubilization of or­
ganics such as aromatic proteins (region II) and SMP (region IV) from 
the primary sludge [55]. 
3.2. Individual fermentation processes and N distribution of the batch 
experiment 
3.2.1. Hydrolysis, acetogenesis and methanogenesis processes 
Micro-aeration was reported to facilitate hydrolysis process in 
anaerobic fermentation [24]. It can also benefit methane production, 
resulting in strong and continuous VFA consumption [35]. Therefore, it 
is necessary to explore the role of micro-aeration in the hydrolysis, 
acetogenesis and methanogenesis steps. Considering that the protein 
was much higher than the carbohydrate (Fig. 1d), protease activity was 
chosen as a measure to reveal the activity of hydrolysis process [57]. In 
addition, activities of enzymes acetate kinase (AK) and coenzyme F420 
(F420) were obtained to characterize the activities of the acetogenesis 
and methanogenesis processes, respectively (Fig. 3). The protease ac­
tivity with micro-aeration was consistently higher than in the control 
group (Fig. 3a), indicating that the presence of oxygen did promote the 
hydrolysis process of primary sludge. This is consistent with the rapid 
decrease of soluble protein observed earlier (Fig. 2b). Similarly, the AK 
activities in the micro-aeration group were higher than the control 
group (on Day 1 and 3) (Fig. 3b), suggesting that the acetogenesis pro­
cess was enhanced in the presence of tiny amounts of O2. However, on 
day 9, the AK activity of the micro-aeration group was lower than in the 
control group, possibly due to insufficient substrates (i.e., proteins and 
carbohydrates). In general, these observations implied that micro- 
aeration was beneficial for promoting both the hydrolysis and aceto­
genesis process. 
Both the methane production and F420 activity were monitored to 
reveal the impact of micro-aeration on the methane production. As 
depicted in Fig. 3c, the cumulative methane production in the micro- 
aeration group (8.03 mL) was much higher than the control group 
(3.87 mL). This, coupled with the reduced VFAs concentration (Fig. 1), 
revealing an enhancement of methanogenic activity due to micro- 
aeration. Additionally, the VFAs consumption would result in pH 
decrease over time, creating a more suitable environment for the 
methanogens [43]. Meanwhile, the F420 activities gradually increased 
over time in both groups, and the micro-aeration group showed a rela­
tively higher F420 activity than that in the control group (Fig. 3d). 
Notably, F420 was a key enzyme involved in hydrogenotrophic meth­
anogenesis [28], indicating that the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis 
was also improved with micro-aeration. Collectively, the above obser­
vations implied that application of micro-aeration promoted all pro­
cesses including hydrolysis, acetogenesis and methanogenesis. 
3.2.2. Effect of micro-aeration on microbial activity 
To further explore the influence of micro-aeration on microbial ac­
tivities, catalase (CAT) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activities 
during the fermentation were further determined. As demonstrated by 
the observation of CAT activities in Fig. 3e, the intervention of micro- 
aeration may lead to the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), 
thus resulting in higher CAT activity in the presence of micro-aeration 
[54]. Similarly, the introduction of micro-aeration also increased the 
LDH activity in the reactor (Fig. 3f). As proper ROS level could stimulate 
the physiological activity [28,60], the ROS induced by micro-aeration 
might improve the microbial activity, thus contributing to enhanced 
anaerobic fermentation processes as discussed above. 
3.2.3. Nitrogen distribution in the anaerobic system 
The distribution of N during the fermentation was further investi­
gated (Fig. S3a). The soluble NH4
+-N in the control group gradually 
increased and reached a maximum value of 379.2 mg/L on day 9. 
However, little NO3
−-N or NO2
−-N was detected during the whole 
fermentation. Interestingly, the maximal concentration of soluble NH4
+- 
N in the micro-aeration group (286.8 mg/L, day 9) was only about 75.6 
% of that in the control group. A possible explanation may be that the 
introduction of O2 could create aerobic-anoxic-anaerobic micro-envi­
ronments within the serum bottles, resulting in simultaneous nitrifica­
tion and denitrification [61]. After fermentation, the N distribution in 
the solid and liquid phase was determined (Fig. S3b). The solid phase N 
fraction after fermentation in both groups were significantly lower than 
the influent. This could be attributed to decomposition of organic sub­
stances (e.g., proteins) during which soluble NH4
+-N was produced [41]. 
Since micro-aeration promoted the hydrolysis process, more N should be 
released from the solid phase of the sludge. Indeed, a lower solid phase N 
concentration was observed in micro-aeration group (611.1 mg/L) than 
that in the control group (672.8 mg/L). In addition, the micro-aeration 
group accumulated more NO2
−-N (3.81 mg/L) in the supernatant than 
the control group (0.14 mg/L). It was reported that NO2
−-N usually 
accumulated attributing to electron competition between nitrate 
reductase and nitrite reductase [11]. Hence, the higher NO2
−-N and NO3
−- 
N level further support the hypothesis that micro-aeration promoted 
simultaneous nitrification and denitrification in this system. 
Theoretically, 2.86 mg COD is required to remove 1 mg NO3
−-N 
during denitrification [48]. At the end of fermentation, the total N 
concentration (i.e., NO3
−-N + NO2
−-N + NH4
+-N + TN-solid) in micro- 
aeration group was 131.6 mg/L lower than in the control group 
(Fig. S3b). Assuming that all 131.6 mg/L of N was converted to NO3
−-N, 
the denitrification process of those NO3
−-N would theoretically require 
376.4 mg COD/L carbon source. However, compared with the control 
group, the VFA and SCOD in micro-aeration group were reduced by 
832.1 mg COD/L and 1701.8 mg/L, respectively (Fig. 1). Hence, a large 
faction of VFA and SCOD may be consumed by other microbial activities 
such as methane production and aerobic respiration. 
3.3. Anaerobic fermentation performance in semi-continuous reactors 
3.3.1. VFAs production performance 
To evaluate the effect of micro-aeration on VFA accumulation under 
semi-continuous mode, VFAs concentrations were measured over time 
(Fig. 5). In the batch experiment above, it was observed that CH4 pro­
duction in the micro-aeration group was significantly increased over the 
control group (Fig. 3f). Shorter SRTs are commonly regarded as more 
conducive for VFA accumulation by mitigating the influence of metha­
nogens [1,46]. Therefore, a short SRT (3 d) was optimized in advance 
and adopted in the semi-continuous experiment. VFA production in the 
semi-continuous reactors are illustrated in Fig. 4. The VFA production in 
both reactors increased at first, and decreased after day 10 onwards due 
to fluctuations of the influent (Fig. 4a), and finally re-increased gradu­
ally until stabilizing from around day 24. During the steady stage, the 
VFA concentration in the micro-aeration group reached 1343.6 mg 
COD/L, while the control group reached 1645.8 mg COD/L. Compared 
to the influent, the effluent VFA in the micro-aeration and control groups 
increased by 91.0 % and 134.0 %, respectively (Fig. S4). Compared to 
the VFA reduction in batch experiment (832.1 mg COD/L), VFA in 
micro-aeration group was only about 300 mg COD/L lower than that in 
the control, indicating that short SRT might reduce VFA consumption by 
methanogens. 
Moreover, soluble nitrogen and phosphorus during the operation 
were also monitored (Fig. 4b, c). Initially, the soluble PO4
3−-P concen­
trations in both groups accumulated rapidly, and reached their peaks 
around 70 mg/L on day 3. This could be attributed to phosphate release 
during the fermentation. Then, the soluble PO4
3−-P further declined to 
39.8 mg/L and 33.4 mg/L on day 15 in the control and micro-aeration

micro-aeration groups increased gradually and stabilized at 57.7 mg/L

+-N concentrations fol­

P in the fermentation broth. 
3.3.2. Key enzymes and microbial activities 
The activities of key enzymes were determined on day 30 when the 
semi-continuous reactors were operated stably (Fig. 5). The activities of 
protease and AK in the micro-aeration group increased by 53.3 % and 
12.1 % respectively compared to the control group (Fig. 5a, b), indi­
cating enhanced hydrolysis and acetogenesis activities. As for meth­
anogenesis, F420 and acetyl-coenzyme A synthase (ACS) are key 
enzymes in hydrogenotrophic and acetoclastic methanogenesis, 
respectively [28]. During the acetoclastic methanogenesis, acetate is 
first converted into acetyl-coenzyme A, followed by ACS dependent 
hydroxylation, a key step to transform acetate into methane [8]. As 
shown in Fig. 5c, d, micro-aeration improved both the activities of F420 
and ACS, with the activities increased by 23.3 % (F420) and 33.8 % 
(ACS) compared to the control. It clearly implied that micro-aeration 
can 
promote 
both 
the 
hydrogenotrophic 
and 
acetoclastic 
methanogenesis, which was also observed in the batch experiment. 
Moreover, the activities of CAT and LDH (Fig. 5e, f) were also improved 
similar to the results obtained in the batch experiments. Together with 
the high functional enzymes’ activities, it indicated that the micro- 
aeration stimulated and enhanced the overall microbial activities. 
3.3.3. Carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus balance 
After the reactor was stabilized, carbon and nitrogen balances were 
established based on their total content in the corresponding reactor 
(Fig. 6). The carbon content in the solid, liquid, and gas phases of sludge 
was shown in Fig. 6a. It was found that the majority of carbon was still 
present in the solid phase. In the micro-aeration group, solids accounted 
only 63 % of the carbon content (80 % in the control), revealing that 
micro-aeration did promote the solubilization of the solids. The carbon 
contents in the liquid phase and CH4 were similar in both groups, further 
implied that VFA consumption by methanogens was alleviated. Inter­
estingly, the carbon content distributed in “others” with micro-aeration 
(18 %) was much higher than that in the control (2 %), which may be 
due to respiration by faculty bacteria and denitrification [10]. As for 
nitrogen (Fig. 6b), the introduction of micro-aeration resulted in more N 
released from the solid phase, and TN concentrations in the solid phase 
was 558.0 mg/L (control) and 521.7 mg/L (micro-aeration), respec­
tively. However, the liquid phase NH4
+-N concentration of 297.4 mg/L in 
the control group was higher than that in the micro-aeration group 
(251.7 mg/L). Similar to the batch experiment, the slight accumulation 
of NO2
−-N indicated that nitrification and denitrification were promoted

As for phosphorus, the total phosphorus (TP) amount was similar in

However, the TP in the solid phase was much higher in the micro-

agreement with the lower soluble PO4

variations of P distribution in the solid phase. It was found that increased 
organic-P in solids (42 % in micro-aeration versus 39 % in control) 
mainly accounted for the P increase in sludge solids. The above results 
indicated that application of micro-aeration didn’t change the TP but the 
distribution of P. 
3.4. Microbial characteristics of the semi-continuous reactor 
3.4.1. Microbial community structure 
The microbial community structure at phylum and genus levels are 
further depicted in Fig. 7. As shown in Fig. 7a, Phyla Actinobacteriota, 
Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Chloroflexi were the main phyla which 
were commonly detected in anaerobic reactors [15]. Among them, the 
VFA consuming Phylum Proteobacteria increased from 31.53 % (control) 
to 43.59 % (micro-aeration), which explains the relatively low VFA 
content in the micro-aeration group [16]. Phylum Firmicutes relating to 
hydrolysis and acidification increased from 10.02 % (control) to 12.96 
% (micro-aeration) [62]. The bacterial community at genus level was 
shown in Fig. 7b. Genus Acinetobacter relating to hydrolysis was the most 
dominant genus in micro-aeration reactor with a relative abundance of 
35.44 % (versus 19.92 % in the control) [40]. In addition, some species 
from this genus was also reported to be polyphosphate accumulating 
organisms (PAOs) [22]. Another dominant genus Candidatus_Microthrix 
relating to removal of organic pollutants, TN, and phosphate accounted 
for abundances of 16.45 % (control) and 14.4 % (micro-aeration), 
respectively [27,32]. The distribution of archaea is depicted in Fig. 7c. 
Acetoclastic methanogens are mainly composed of Methanosarcina and 
Methanosaeta [28,42], Methanosaeta occupied similar abundances in the 
control (30.72 %) and micro-aeration (28.79 %) groups. However, 
higher relative abundance of hydrogenotrophic Methanobrevibacter was 
observed in micro-aeration group (32.31 %) than the control (17.75 %), 
indicating that micro-aeration enriched the methanogens capable of 
utilizing H2.

During anaerobic fermentation, micro-aeration might induce ROS

Group were 123.79 % and 105.90 % of those in the control group, 
respectively. This was in accordance with the higher hydrolysis enzymes 
activities (Fig. 5a). After hydrolysis, the produced low molecular weight 
organics would be further bio-converted into acetate by AK [23]. The 
abundance of AK (EC: 2.7.2.1) gene in the micro-aeration group was 
about 121.40 % of that in the control group. Clearly, the acetogenesis 
activity was also improved by micro-aeration, consistent with the AK 
activity (Fig. 5b).

anogenesis pathways exhibited in KEGG database were detected (Fig. 8).

3.5. N and P transformation pathway in the semi-continuous reactor 
During the fermentation, N and P from solid phase would be released 
into the liquid phase (Fig. 4), which might pose negative effects on the 
subsequent process. Hence, the N and P transformation pathways in 
current systems were then analyzed. Based on the metagenomic results, 
both nitrification and denitrification genes were detected in the reactors. 
It indicates the possibility of simultaneous occurrence of nitrification 
and denitrification processes. On the one hand, the abundances of 
nitrification genes increased in the presence of micro-aeration (Fig. 9a). 
Compared to the control group, the abundances of ammonia mono­
oxygenase (EC: 1.14.99.39) and hydroxylamine dehydrogenase (EC: 
1.7.2.6) genes increased by 89.72 % and 46.13 %, respectively. This 
result could explain the relatively lower ammonia (Fig. 4c) and higher 
NO2
−-N (Table S6) concentrations in the micro-aeration group than the 
control group. However, similar gene abundances of nitrite oxidore­
ductase (EC: 1.7.99.-) were observed in both reactors. On the other 
hand, the denitrification genes were also detected with higher abun­
dances in the micro-aeration group. For example, the abundances of 
functional genes encoding nitric oxide reductase (EC: 1.7.2.5), and 
nitrous oxide reductase (EC: 1.7.2.4) in the micro-aeration group 
increased by 63.45 %, and 41.91 % compared to the control group, 
respectively. It indicated that micro-aeration also enhanced the deni­
trification process which decreased the total nitrogen content of the 
system. 
To better exhibit the effect of micro-aeration on nitrogen meta­
bolism, the genes’ abundances affiliated to different nitrogen meta­
bolism pathway are illustrated in Fig. 9b, c. The nitrification and 
denitrification genes displayed higher abundances among these path­
ways, and both pathways’ genes were upregulated by micro-aeration. 
From another point of view, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle is the 
central metabolic pathway of carbon, through which the electrons are 
mainly produced [51]. It is also regarded as the energy center of deni­
trifying bacteria, providing the reducing power of the electron transfer 
chain and the synthetic metabolic substrates for cell growth [14,26]. 
Thus, the genes encoding TCA enzymes were further investigated 
(Fig. 9e, f). Within this pathway, the abundance of gene encoding suc­
cinate dehydrogenase (EC: 1.3.5.1) increased by 65.37 % with micro- 
aeration compared to the control group, indicating higher activities of 
carbon metabolism and reducing power production. Considering the 
relatively lower VFA concentration and upregulated denitrification 
pathway with micro-aeration, it further indicated that the micro- 
aeration might improve VFA consumption via TCA cycle, providing 
more reducing power for microbial denitrification. 
As for the phosphorus metabolism, polyphosphate kinase 1 (PPK1) 
and polyphosphate kinase 2 (PPK2) genes were the dominant functional 
genes [7,20]. Specifically, PPK1 is involved in polyphosphate (poly-P) 
formation in PAOs, while PPK2 hydrolyzes poly-P to synthesize GTP 
(Guanosine triphosphate) [7,36]. The relative abundance of PPK1 gene 
wasn’t impacted much by the micro-aeration, while that of PPK2 gene 
decreased by 35.0 % compared to the control group. The phosphate 
hydrolase (PPX) is another enzyme responsible for the hydrolysis of 
poly-P (Fig. 9d) [31,36]. The PPX gene encoding this enzyme was also 
down-regulated by the micro-aeration (0.063 % vs. 0.075 % in the 
control). It indicated that the degradation of poly-P was inhibited by 
micro-aeration, which was in accordance with the observed high P 
content in the solid phase. Moreover, the alkaline phosphatase D (phoD) 
gene is related to organic-P mineralization, and the abundance of this 
gene was significantly reduced by micro-aeration (0.043 % vs. 0.065 % 
in control). Considering the higher organic-P distribution in solid phase, 
these results indicated that micro-aeration inhibit both extracellular 
organic-P mineralization and intracellular poly-P degradation, resulting 
in the lower soluble PO4
3−-P. 
Overall, the soluble NH4
+-N and PO4
3−-P concentrations in the 
fermentation broth were significantly reduced by micro-aeration. 
Considering that micro-aeration is regarded as a simple and econom­
ical approach that could be used in anaerobic system [10], engineering 
application of this technology is also expected to be technically feasible. 
However, most studies relating to micro-aeration is still limited to the 
laboratory scale [23,52], and the economic evaluation of micro-aeration 
technology is still lacking [10]. Hence, the anaerobic fermentation 
performance as well as economic characteristics adopting this technol­
ogy in pilot and full scale still have to be comprehensively evaluated in 
the future study. Besides, several other limitations and challenges also 
need to be addressed before future industrial applications of this tech­
nology. For example, different influence pattern of micro-aeration on 
anaerobic fermentation were observed in different studies [35,52]. 
Hence, the oxygen dosage and micro-aeration pattern need to be further 
optimized for higher production of VFA and better control of soluble N 
and P. Considering the low solubility and poor mass transfer of oxygen 
into liquid phase, development of an efficient oxygen dosing method is 
also anticipated. In addition, hydrodynamics and mass transport will 
vary greatly during the scaling up process compared to the laboratory 
scale reactors. Hence, some other methods including hydrodynamics 
modeling should be incorporated for reactor design and optimization 
during further industrial applications. 
4. Conclusion 
This study systematically investigated the influence of micro- 
aeration on anaerobic VFAs production from primary sludge as well as 
the simultaneous N and P transformations. The specific conclusions are 
follows:  
(1) The micro-aeration exhibited a non-targeted improvement effect 
on the anaerobic fermentation of primary sludge, including hy­
drolysis, acetogenesis, and methanogenesis processes. The over­
all microbial activity was also enhanced by micro-aeration as 
evidenced by the higher functional enzymes’ activities. 
(2) The micro-aeration enriched hydrogenotrophic genus Methano­
brevibacter of the archaeal community and genus Acinetobacter of 
the bacterial community. However, the acetoclastic methano­
genesis was still the dominant CH4 production pathway that 
consumed VFA at the gene level.  
(3) Compared to control, the application of micro-aeration could 
remove 131.6 mg/L more N in the system, and soluble NH4
+-N 
was also reduced by it during the anaerobic fermentation. The 
occurrence of simultaneous nitrification and denitrification was 
found to be responsible for the total N loss of this system.  
(4) The total P content in the reactor remained unchanged, while 
more P was distributed in the organic-P within the sludge solids 
(1.91 mg/g vs. 1.56 mg/g in the control). It could be attributed to 
that the micro-aeration inhibited both extracellular organic-P 
mineralization and intracellular poly-P degradation, resulting in 
more P retained in the solids phase. 
Overall, this study demonstrated that micro-aeration could induce 
simultaneous transformation of soluble N and P during the anaerobic 
fermentation of primary sludge. These results could help to inform 
future design of fermentation processes, and to optimize for both N and 
P release using micro-aeration.
